theme: How long?, and: the LORD looks down from heaven
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 13 and Psalm 14. Psalm 13 is a short lament that ends in trust, and Psalm 14 describes the state of humanity without God. Read the two together.
settingTheScene: Both psalms are attributed to David. Psalm 13 is the shortest of the great laments, with only six verses, and many readers have found that it expresses the experience of waiting on God better than any other. Psalm 14 is a sober assessment of human sin, which Paul quotes in Romans 3. They are paired in the Psalter, and here they sit during David’s years on the run, when answers were slow to come.
observation: “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?” (13:1).
“How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day?” (13:2).
“Light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death” (13:3).
“But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation” (13:5).
“I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me” (13:6).
“The fool says in his heart, There is no God” (14:1).
“The LORD looks down from heaven on the children of man, to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God” (14:2).
“They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one” (14:3).
interpretation:
The structure of Psalm 13 is a model for lament. First comes the complaint, four times repeated: “How long?” David feels forgotten, hidden from, and abandoned in his own thoughts. Second comes the request: “Consider and answer me, O LORD my God.” Third comes the turn: “But I have trusted in your steadfast love.” The final line is a vow of praise.

The turn is the key. Nothing has changed in David’s situation. There is no explanation of how the enemy will be defeated. What changes is that David decides to trust. The word “trusted” is in the past tense, as though he were holding on to what he already knows. He recalls the covenant love of God and remembers that he has been dealt with bountifully before. Lament leads to trust not by getting answers, but by returning to what God has already revealed about himself.

Psalm 14 is darker. The fool, in the Bible, is not someone of low intelligence but a person who lives as though there were no God. The fool says it “in his heart,” meaning that it is a practical atheism more than a formal argument. The result is corruption. The psalm describes God looking down over the whole human race and finding no one who seeks him.

This is a hard truth, and it is the basis of the gospel. “There is none who does good, not even one.” Human beings cannot find their own way to God. Paul uses these lines in Romans 3 to prove that all, Jew and Gentile, are under sin.

Yet the psalm ends with hope: “Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion!” If humans cannot save themselves, then salvation must come from God. And the psalm says that God is “the refuge” of the poor and that he is with the generation of the righteous.
connection: Paul quotes Psalm 14:1-3 in Romans 3:10-12 to show that all are under sin, and then shows that God’s righteousness comes by faith in Christ (Romans 3:21-26). Salvation did come out of Zion in Jesus (Romans 11:26). Jesus cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46) so that we might never be forsaken. Ephesians 2:4-5 says that God, being rich in mercy, made us alive.
application:
If you are in a long season of waiting, pray Psalm 13 aloud as your own.

Notice where you live as a practical atheist, making plans without God.

Thank God that salvation did come out of Zion.
prayerPrompts: Tell God how long you have been waiting, and what for.
Confess where you have lived as though there were no God.
